title: By grace, not of yourselves (Ephesians 2:8–10)
hook: saved by grace through faith, created for good works

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crushing weight and an everyday pack. Your line was bear one another. Whose corner did you lift? Day five hundred eighty-three.

On October thirty-first, 1999, in the German city of Augsburg, representatives of the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration. It was about a question that had divided them since the sixteenth century: how is a person made right with God? Today's verses sat near the center of that long argument. They come from Ephesians, the first of a new stretch of letters. Tradition says Paul wrote them as a prisoner, in chains.
screen: `AUGSBURG, OCTOBER 1999.` → `AN ARGUMENT FIVE CENTURIES OLD.` → `LETTERS FROM PRISON.`

segments.voice: Ephesians chapter two starts with a hard picture: you were dead in your sins. Then the turn: God, who is rich in mercy, brought us to life with Christ. Then the verses: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God; Not of works, that no man may glory." A gift. Not wages. Nobody can take credit for it. But Paul doesn't stop there, and this is where readers who quote only verse eight miss half the sentence: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus in good works, which God hath prepared that we should walk in them." Saved by grace, and made for good works. Not saved by good works, and not saved from doing them. The works were prepared in advance, like a path laid down for you to walk on. The Greek word for workmanship is poiēma, something made. The English word poem comes from it, though here it just means God's handiwork. Catholics and Protestants argued for centuries over how grace, faith and works fit together. The Catholic Church taught at the Council of Trent that nothing before justification, neither faith nor works, earns the grace of justification. And in the 1999 declaration, Catholics and Lutherans said together that by grace alone, in faith in Christ, and not because of any merit, we are accepted by God, who renews our hearts and calls us to good works. Some differences remain, and both sides say so. But on this, they found they could speak with one voice.
screen: `DEAD, THEN MADE ALIVE.` · `A GIFT, NOT WAGES.` · `HIS WORKMANSHIP: POIĒMA.` · `CATHOLICS AND LUTHERANS, 1999.` · then, large: `BY GRACE YOU ARE SAVED THROUGH FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive, then do. Settle, and breathe. Turn your hands palm up on your knees, the way you'd hold them to receive something. Stay like that for a few breaths. Think of one good thing in your life you didn't earn: a person, your health, a morning, your faith if you have it. Let it be a gift. Then turn your hands over, ready to work. Think of one good thing you could do today that seems to be waiting for you. If you pray, you can thank God, then ask for help to do it. If you don't, simply receive, then decide. The bell holds the time.
By grace. Paul's words to the Ephesians: saved by God's gift, not by works, and then made for the good works God prepared. Today's word.
Your line: his workmanship. Today, do one good thing that seems to have been waiting for you, and think of it as a path, not a payment. Day five hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics teach that justification is a free gift of grace that no one can merit, and that grace also makes good works possible; in 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration on justification.

original.note: Greek: something made, a work (Ephesians 2:10). English 'poem' comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Protestant slogan about faith alone.
what it means: salvation is God's gift, received in faith, and it makes us his handiwork, made for good works.
what a scholar hears: poiēma, God's 'thing made'; Trent, Session 6, chapter 8; the 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification.

notes: Joint Declaration signed 31 October 1999 in Augsburg by the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church (Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity). JDDJ 15 paraphrased. Confirm.
Trent Session 6, chapter 8 paraphrased ('none of those things which precede justification, whether faith or works, merit the grace itself of justification'). Confirm.
Ephesians as a 'captivity letter' (3:1, 4:1, 6:20) stated as tradition; many scholars debate Pauline authorship of Ephesians. Keeper may want a note.
poiēma → poem: standard etymology; the script explicitly says the verse simply means 'handiwork'.
